caution: Charcoal production releases carbon monoxide, an invisible, odorless, toxic gas. Always burn outdoors with good airflow, never in an enclosed or poorly ventilated space.

claims.claim: Charcoal is made by heating wood in a low-oxygen environment, a process called pyrolysis, which drives off water and volatile compounds and leaves behind mostly carbon.
claims.source: General chemistry/materials knowledge on pyrolysis and charcoal production; independently documented, not book-derived.

claims.claim: Traditional charcoal burners built earth-covered mounds of wood that smoldered slowly for days, using small vents to carefully limit the amount of air reaching the fire.
claims.source: General historical-craft knowledge of traditional charcoal-mound (kiln/pit) burning; independently documented, not book-derived.

claims.claim: Because ordinary burning wood needs oxygen, the mound has to be sealed with earth, turf, or clay so the fire smolders instead of fully combusting into ash.
claims.source: General chemistry/craft knowledge on controlled-oxygen combustion; independently documented, not book-derived.

claims.claim: Finished charcoal burns hotter and cleaner than raw wood because much of the water, tar, and volatile gas has already been driven off during the burn.
claims.source: General materials-science knowledge on charcoal versus raw wood combustion; independently documented, not book-derived.

claims.claim: Charcoal burning produces carbon monoxide, an invisible and odorless toxic gas, so it must always be done outdoors with good ventilation and never inside an enclosed space.
claims.source: General chemical-safety knowledge on carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion; independently documented, not book-derived.

claims.claim: Charcoal burners traditionally judged progress by smoke color: thick white smoke means water and volatiles are still cooking off, while thin blue smoke signals the burn is nearly done and the mound should be sealed to smother it.
claims.source: General historical-craft knowledge of traditional charcoal-burning technique; independently documented, not book-derived.
